terms.definition: A function that turns any input into a fixed-size number, spreading inputs evenly across the range.
The remainder after division; hashing a key and taking it modulo N picks one of N slots.
One server in a group, such as one cache or one database shard.

before.note: Read Caching first: consistent hashing is how a cache or data cluster decides which node holds each key. The terms below are enough to begin.

stages.name: Basics
body: When data is spread across several nodes, something has to decide which node holds each key. The obvious way is to hash the key and take it modulo the number of nodes. That works until the number of nodes changes: add or remove one, and almost every key now maps to a different node, so nearly all the data has to move at once. Karger and colleagues, who introduced consistent hashing, define a consistent hash function as one that changes minimally as the range of the function changes [[karger]].

Consistent hashing was designed to fix exactly this. In the original paper both buckets and items are mapped at random onto the unit interval, and each item goes to the closest bucket [[karger]]. Dynamo describes the ring version that many systems copy: the output of the hash function is treated as a fixed circular space, each node is given a random position on it, and a key is stored on the first node found walking clockwise from the key's position [[dynamo]].

The payoff is that very little moves. Dynamo says the arrival or departure of a node only affects its immediate neighbours, and other nodes remain unaffected [[dynamo]]. The original paper states the guarantees as properties: balance, where each bucket gets about 1/|V| of the items, and monotonicity, where adding buckets moves items only onto the new buckets [[karger]]. That is what makes it possible to grow or shrink a cluster without a storm of data movement.

stages.name: How it works
body: Picture the hash values as points around a circle. Each node is hashed to a point on the circle. To place a key, hash it to its own point, then walk clockwise until you meet a node; that node owns the key [[dynamo]]. Looking up a key means hashing it and finding that same next node.

Adding a node drops a new point on the circle. Each node is responsible for the region of the ring between it and its predecessor, so the new node takes over only the keys that fall in that region; every other key is untouched. Removing a node hands its keys to the next node clockwise, and again nothing else moves [[dynamo]]. This locality is the whole point.

A plain ring can be lumpy. Dynamo names two challenges with the basic algorithm: the random position of each node leads to non-uniform data and load distribution, and it ignores differences in node performance. Its answer is virtual nodes: each physical node is assigned multiple points on the ring, so the load evens out and a node that leaves spreads its keys across many others rather than one neighbour [[dynamo]].

The original construction assumes two random functions, one mapping buckets to the unit interval and one mapping items, which is why the quality of the spread depends on the hash function being well distributed [[karger]].

terms.definition: Finding a key's owner by moving around the ring from the key to the next node.
One of many ring points assigned to a single physical node to even out load.
The span of the ring between two adjacent node points; the keys in it belong to the node ahead.
How evenly keys are spread across nodes; virtual nodes make it more even.
The limited movement of keys to new owners when a node joins or leaves.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: Consistent hashing is usually paired with replication. A key is not only stored on its owning node but also on the next few nodes clockwise, so if the owner fails the data is still reachable. The ring doubles as the way to find the backups: they are simply the following nodes [[dynamo]].

Where the ring is managed differs by system. Dynamo-style systems let every node work out which nodes should hold a key, so requests can be routed without a central coordinator [[dynamo]]. Redis Cluster does not use consistent hashing at all. Its page says every key is part of a hash slot, there are 16384 slots, the slot is the CRC16 of the key modulo 16384, and every node is responsible for a subset of the slots [[redis-cluster]]. That keeps the mapping explicit and lets you move data slot by slot.

Even with virtual nodes, load can be uneven if some keys are far hotter than others, a hot key problem the ring alone does not solve. A single wildly popular key still lands on one node. Handling that needs extra tactics such as replicating or splitting the hot key, which is a caching and sharding concern layered on top of the ring. This is general background; the pages cited here do not discuss hot keys.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: The main trade-off is between even load and simplicity. More virtual nodes per machine give a smoother spread but cost more memory and bookkeeping to track all the ring points. Fixed hash slots, as in Redis Cluster, give an explicit mapping that you can move in fixed units; the page's reshard command asks how many slots you want to move, from 1 to 16384 [[redis-cluster]].

Consistent hashing shines when the node set changes often, which is the normal state of a large cache or store: machines fail, get replaced, and are added as traffic grows. If your node set never changed, plain modulo hashing would be fine; the technique earns its complexity because real clusters are always churning.

This idea connects the map. It is how a cache cluster, the previous topic, decides which cache holds a key, and it is one of the ways a sharded database, a later topic, decides which shard holds a row. Learning it here means replication and sharding will reuse the same ring rather than introduce it fresh.

misconceptions.myth: Consistent hashing spreads keys perfectly evenly.
misconceptions.truth: Dynamo says the basic ring leads to non-uniform data and load distribution, and uses virtual nodes to even it out [[dynamo]].

misconceptions.myth: Adding a node reshuffles all the data.
misconceptions.truth: Dynamo says the arrival or departure of a node only affects its immediate neighbours [[dynamo]].

misconceptions.myth: The ring removes hot spots entirely.
misconceptions.truth: A single very popular key still lands on one node, so hot keys need extra handling.

misconceptions.myth: Every system places keys by walking a continuous ring.
misconceptions.truth: Redis Cluster does not use consistent hashing; it assigns keys to 16384 hash slots and slots to nodes [[redis-cluster]].
